Eye Movement Simulator

What does “tilt recruitment” mean?

Head tilt activates vestibular pathways that recruit the cyclovertical extraocular muscles to counterrotate the eyes. The simulator adds an illustrative activation increment to the relevant muscle sliders, shown as “tilt recruitment.”

For right head tilt, the model increases right superior rectus/superior oblique and left inferior rectus/inferior oblique recruitment; left tilt reverses this pattern. With a CN IV palsy, the affected superior oblique cannot contribute normally, so compensatory recruitment of the superior rectus may worsen hypertropia.

Important: These percentages are not measured muscle firing rates or forces. Slider position represents modeled neural recruitment; the colored action buttons separately indicate relative gaze-dependent mechanical effectiveness.

ⓘ About action colors and isolation

Action color intensity changes with gaze. During head tilt, vestibular recruitment is represented by increased activation in the relevant cyclovertical muscle bars, not by extra pink highlighting of torsional actions. Action colors continue to represent gaze-dependent mechanical effectiveness. Medial and lateral rectus sole horizontal actions stay fully highlighted; yellow tertiary horizontal actions stay deliberately subdued and vary only subtly; their peak is not experimentally calibrated. Vertical recti elevate/depress most effectively in abduction and show more torsional action in adduction; obliques depress/elevate most effectively in adduction and show more torsional action in abduction. Primary gaze is intermediate. These are relative action weights, not absolute force. The display is illustrative, not a calibrated measurement. Isolation affects only the selected muscle and action.

Pathology
Palsy simulation

CN III patterns are illustrative: pupil-sparing refers to preserved pupillary function despite motor weakness. Pupil-only dysfunction has no extraocular muscle weakness. Pupil findings alone do not establish cause or exclude aneurysm; acute suspected CN III palsy requires urgent clinical assessment.

Sliders represent illustrative relative neural drive, not measured muscle force. In primary gaze, opposing tonic forces cancel; weakness removes their contribution and produces an illustrative resting deviation. In CN IV palsy, ipsilateral head tilt increases the affected superior rectus drive (intorsion plus elevation); contralateral tilt increases inferior rectus drive (extorsion plus depression), reducing hypertropia. Both changes are qualitative teaching approximations, not measured neural activity.

Comitant Strabismus

CN VI integration: Selecting a unilateral CN VI palsy automatically activates a gaze-dependent esotropia (illustrative 2Δ away, 6Δ primary, 20Δ toward the paretic lateral rectus). The cover paddle and base-out prisms now operate on this deviation. Covering the healthy eye switches fixation to the paretic eye, producing a larger fellow-eye secondary deviation under Hering’s law. This teaching model does not simulate a measured patient-specific deviation or full mechanical abduction limits. Horizontal and vertical prism components may be stacked over the same eye. In CN III palsy, the vertical hypotropia now changes with upgaze, downgaze, and horizontal gaze; prism neutralization follows the current gaze-dependent vertical deviation. Lift eyelid exposes the eye for examination without curing the underlying ptosis.

Pick up the occluder and move it over an eye to perform cover–uncover testing; move back and forth to perform an alternate cover test. In this simplified teaching mode, a phoria produces no visible refixation during a single cover–uncover cycle; quickly alternate the occluder between eyes to break fusion and reveal a refixation movement. For tropias, the affected eye has a manifest deviation and may refixate when the fellow eye is covered. For horizontal deviations, the same base direction corrects the deviation with a prism over either eye (base-in for exo, base-out for eso); for vertical deviations, the fellow eye requires the opposite vertical base direction. Prism correction is illustrated using the residual deviation: closer matching prism power and base direction reduces the refixation movement. This is a simplified teaching model, not a calibrated binocular fusion simulation.

Complex localization: cavernous sinus / orbital apex

Illustrative localization presets. Each nerve and associated finding can be adjusted independently. CN V is intentionally omitted.

Select a lesion pattern to begin.

Afferent dysfunction is represented by a relative afferent pupillary defect in the swinging-flashlight model, not by a fixed dilated pupil. Disc edema, pallor, and a normal-appearing disc can occur with optic neuropathy. Orbital congestion is a schematic frontal projection, not true Hertel exophthalmometry. External fundus examples require an internet connection.

Nystagmus and saccadic oscillations
Fixation ON (F button beside primary gaze)

Fixation button simulates visual fixation versus fixation removed. Both components can be edited independently and summed. Oscillations are visual overlays; the underlying lesion and cover-test measurements are unchanged.

Eye-position traces

Solid: right eye; dashed: left eye. Horizontal, vertical, and torsional traces use separate scales and are illustrative.

Select a preset or enable a component.

Foveation fraction is the proportion of each jerk cycle held near the foveal target (illustrative plateau, not a full waveform reconstruction). Interocular phase shifts the left-eye oscillation relative to the right; left-eye amplitude ratio = left amplitude ÷ right amplitude (1 means equal). Ocular flutter uses smooth back-to-back simulated saccades without an intersaccadic pause. Rebound requires eccentric gaze followed by return to primary; hold longer for a stronger transient reversal.

Supranuclear Gaze Disorders
Use the Voluntary / VOR switch in the examination tools above to demonstrate preserved reflex gaze.

VOR mode reverses head and eye directions; downward head pitch can demonstrate preserved reflex elevation despite restricted voluntary upgaze. This is a simplified examination maneuver, not a complete head-motion model. Downward-moving OKN stripes evoke upward fast phases and can provoke convergence-retraction bursts in the Parinaud preset.

Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)
Original published figure and Moran CORE examination

INO impairs the adducting eye during contralateral horizontal gaze while the abducting eye may show nystagmus. Mild cases emphasize adduction slowing. Near convergence is separately controlled. This is an illustrative MLF conduction model, not a measured saccade recording.

Ptosis
Ptosis / upper-lid position

A complete CN III palsy automatically produces near-complete upper-lid closure (levator paralysis), overriding manual ptosis controls until the palsy is removed. MRD1 is measured from the corneal light reflex to the central upper-lid margin in primary gaze. The selected value sets the modeled primary-gaze lid position; gaze-dependent lid following is preserved. The model uses an illustrative mm-to-pixel scale. Transparent lids can be enabled above.

Pupil Disorders
Pupillary disordersFlashlight off

Use Lights off between the eyes to compare anisocoria in light and dark. Select Slit lamp to reveal an illustrative magnified view of segmental, vermiform iris movements in an eye with a tonic pupil. RAPD affects the bilateral light response, not resting pupil diameter. Only one RAPD can be modeled at a time.

Select Pick up flashlight, then move your pointer over either iris (including its pupil) to illuminate it. Move between pupils to demonstrate direct and consensual responses and a relative afferent pupillary defect. Click the flashlight button again to put it down. On touchscreens, drag your finger across the irises while the flashlight is active.

Fundus examination: Select Pick up ophthalmoscope, then click or tap either iris to view its normal circular fundus photograph. Move the ophthalmoscope with your mouse or finger; close the fundus view to examine the other eye. The photographs are reference images; a CN IV palsy rotates the affected fundus to illustrate excyclotorsion while the fellow eye remains in its normal orientation. Rotation is illustrative, not a measured clinical angle.

With an RAPD, illuminating the affected eye produces a weaker bilateral constriction than illuminating the healthy eye; when the light swings onto the affected side, both pupils appear to dilate relatively. An isolated RAPD does not create anisocoria. Complete pupil-involving CN III palsy still produces ipsilateral mydriasis and absent efferent light/near response. In darkness, Horner syndrome causes relative miosis (anisocoria greater in dark); a tonic pupil is larger and reacts poorly to light, with relative preservation of near constriction. These are schematic pupil sizes, not diagnostic cutoffs. Complete CN III palsy overrides the pupil disorder selection. Illustrative physiology and diameters.

Generate a hidden case from cranial nerve palsies, INO, pupil disorders, complex localization, comitant strabismus, or nystagmus. Examine the eyes and enter the diagnosis (and side when relevant). The simulator hides diagnostic labels and pathology controls until you reveal the answer.

Sources and model notes

Evidence for static ocular counterroll

  1. Chandrakumar M, et al. Effects of Earth-Fixed vs Head-Fixed Targets on Static Ocular Counterroll. Arch Ophthalmol. 2010;128(4):413–417. Full text. Mean gain approximately 0.141 with earth-fixed and 0.084 with head-fixed targets; response saturates with larger head tilt.
  2. Assessment of ocular counterroll during head tilt using binocular video oculography. PubMed. Reports approximately 13–22% compensation and decreasing gain at greater tilts.
  3. Collewijn H, et al. Human ocular counterroll: assessment of static and dynamic properties from electromagnetic scleral coil recordings. Exp Brain Res. 1985. PubMed. Static gain around 10% up to 20°; dynamic gain can be much higher.
  4. Static ocular counterroll: video-based analysis after minimizing the false-torsion factors. PubMed. Reports variable amplitudes across individuals.

Three-step test and clinical interpretation

  1. American Academy of Ophthalmology EyeWiki. Strabismus Surgery, Cyclovertical. Three-step test, action patterns, and limitations.
  2. NCBI Bookshelf, Strabismus (StatPearls). Clinical description of the three steps.
  3. Chandrakumar et al. (source 1) also describes right head tilt recruiting right intorters (SR and SO), and how right SO weakness can increase right hypertropia during ipsilateral tilt.
  4. Static ocular counterroll reflex in skew deviation. PubMed. Skew deviation can produce abnormal and asymmetric counterroll; the three-step pattern is not specific for isolated SO palsy.

Exactly what the simulator does

Pupillary light and near responses: Both pupils constrict for either eye illuminated (direct and consensual reflex), assuming intact afferent pathways and normal pretectal/Edinger–Westphal circuitry. Near gaze triggers modeled bilateral miosis and medial rectus convergence. A selected complete pupil-involving CN III palsy sets the affected pupil to an illustrative 7.2 mm and removes both responses in that eye; the fellow eye responds normally. Normal baseline 5.3 mm, light 3.0 mm, and near 3.5 mm are illustrative display choices. An illustrative RAPD can be selected in either eye: light in the affected eye yields a weaker bilateral constriction (4.7 mm versus 3.0 mm with normal afferent input), causing relative dilation of both pupils when the flashlight swings onto the affected eye. An isolated RAPD does not cause anisocoria. No realistic pupil response latency, hippus, accommodative lens changes, or anisocoria-in-light-versus-dark protocol is modeled. Not all clinical CN III palsies involve the pupil; pupil sparing is possible.

Ptosis and MRD1: A selected complete CN III palsy automatically simulates levator palpebrae superioris paralysis with near-complete eyelid closure (illustrative MRD1 approximately −1 mm), and temporarily locks the corresponding manual ptosis controls. The previous manual setting is restored when CN III palsy is removed. This is a simplified complete palsy; partial CN III palsies may have variable ptosis. Normal MRD1 is approximately 4–5 mm, measured from the central corneal light reflex to the upper lid margin in primary gaze. Independent right/left ptosis toggles set illustrative primary-position MRD1 values of 1, 2, 3, or 5 mm. A fixed 13 SVG pixels/mm scale converts the change from the 5 mm baseline into upper-lid descent. This is a teaching visualization, not a calibrated millimeter measurement, and it does not simulate Hering’s law, brow compensation, levator function, or ptosis etiology. AAO EyeWiki; University of Iowa EyeRounds.

Visible torsion enhancement: For teaching visibility, the iris texture rotates four times the modeled torsion (limited to 38°), while the numerical torsion readout reports the original model angle. The magnified display is not anatomically scaled. The iris has asymmetrical markers near its exposed horizontal edges so rotation remains visible even with normal lid overlap. The optional partially transparent eyelid overlay reveals otherwise occluded iris portions for teaching; it is not an anatomical appearance.

OCR gain: the adjustable initial gain defaults to 0.15. With the saturating response enabled, the modeled counterroll magnitude is gain × 18 × tanh(|head tilt| / 18) degrees. This mathematical saturation is a teaching choice, not a fitted equation from the cited studies. With saturation disabled, counterroll is gain × |head tilt|. Positive right head tilt produces clockwise iris rotation in this frontal screen view (opposite the apparent head tilt); anatomically the right eye intorts and left eye extorts. Left head tilt produces counterclockwise screen rotation, with right-eye extorsion and left-eye intorsion.

Resting tone: a user-adjustable tonic drive (30% default) is assigned to all six muscles. The model subtracts opposing drive in horizontal, vertical, and torsional axes and introduces a deviation when a muscle is weak or disabled. These are normalized arbitrary units, not EMG recordings, measured muscle force, or empirically determined force–length curves.

Pure vertical gaze torsion: The normal upgaze and downgaze presets subtract the artificial torsional offset caused by unequal illustrative rectus/oblique activation. This approximates the expected absence of conspicuous torsion in normal straight vertical gaze under Listing's law. Muscle-slider changes and palsies can still reveal residual torsion. This is not a full Listing's law or pulley model.

Activation slider interpretation: The displayed percentages are illustrative relative activation commands, not measured muscle force or a quantitative share of gaze displacement. Straight upgaze now increases SR and IO by equal illustrative amounts (+42 percentage points), and straight downgaze similarly increases IR and SO equally. This equality is a teaching convention, not a physiological claim. The simplified model includes a small horizontal tertiary effect (coefficient 0.09): increasing IO alone can create a slight abducting drift, but the size is arbitrary and should not be interpreted as a measured deviation. Gaze presets: right gaze recruits right LR + left MR; left gaze recruits right MR + left LR. Up and down gaze recruit paired vertical muscles, without implying a measured activation ratio. Vertical rectus effectiveness increases in abduction, oblique vertical effectiveness in adduction. These are simplified gaze-dependent weights, not an orbital-pulley simulation.

Three-step CN IV demonstration: isolated SO weakness produces a heuristic baseline and contralateral-gaze hypertropia; ipsilateral head-tilt hypertropia arises from modeled superior rectus recruitment; contralateral head tilt reduces the deviation through modeled inferior rectus recruitment. It demonstrates the qualitative pattern; the degree of hypertropia is not a prediction. The effect is engaged directly by selecting CN IV palsy. With ipsilateral head tilt, the affected superior rectus slider displays a larger *effective* activation (illustrative +35 percentage points at 20°), contributing intorsion and elevation. With contralateral head tilt, the affected inferior rectus slider instead increases (illustrative +24 percentage points at 20°), contributing extorsion and depression, which reduces but need not eliminate the hypertropia. Both increments are arbitrary teaching values, not measured muscle tone, EMG, or a validated inverse solution of individual muscle forces. With either an isolated CN IV palsy selected, head tilt also changes modeled vertical alignment. With no CN IV palsy , head tilt alters torsion only.

Action isolation and highlighting: During head tilt, right-eye SR/SO intorsion and left-eye IR/IO extorsion are highlighted for right tilt (reversed for left tilt). This additional intensity depicts qualitative vestibular recruitment, not a measured change in mechanical effectiveness or activation percentage. Tertiary horizontal actions (rectus adduction and oblique abduction) use a deliberately low-intensity yellow scale with a small continuous illustrative variation; no experimentally validated gaze-dependent maximum is implied. Brightness scales are not comparable between action families. Clicking an action isolates its illustrative horizontal, vertical, or torsional contribution. Brightness varies continuously with horizontal eye position, with separate high-contrast scales for vertical and torsional actions; oblique torsion is emphasized in abduction and vertical rectus torsion in adduction. These weights are qualitative and do not represent measured force curves. Muscle isolation is an educational override, not a physiological claim that one muscle action can be switched off independently of its others.

Head tilt display: For a patient-right head tilt, the viewer-left eye is lower than the viewer-right eye. Both eyes rotate as one rigid facial pair around a shared midpoint on the nose axis (rather than individually about each eye); the separate rectangular skin backgrounds have been removed. Iris counterroll remains modeled separately. This is not a full 3-D head or orbit model. Eye drawing: the upper and lower eyelids overlap and clip the iris, with more pronounced upper-lid descent in downgaze; gaze excursions have been increased for a fuller visual demonstration. Iris torsion is visible via radial texture and an asymmetric dark marker. Globe projection, lid following, scleral exposure, and the enlarged angle-to-pixel mapping are illustrative; they are not calibrated to clinical photographs or population-specific palpebral measurements.

Pupillary model: The Horner and tonic pupil options use illustrative baseline and reflex diameters. Horner anisocoria is larger in the dark; a tonic pupil has a poor light response and a relatively preserved near response (the real response may be slow). Horner syndrome also lowers the upper lid by an illustrative 1 mm (mild ptosis). The slit-lamp option draws a schematic animated inset of sectoral/vermiform iris movement for a tonic pupil; it does not reproduce a real slit-lamp video. No pharmacological tests or dynamic dilation lag are simulated. Interpretation: the Parks–Bielschowsky test is a clinical localization aid, not a definitive diagnostic test. Restrictive strabismus, skew deviation, multiple palsies, myasthenia gravis, and previous surgery can confound it. Ocular counterroll varies with viewing condition, head angle, individual, and dynamic versus static tilt. Do not use the simulator to diagnose patients or infer real muscle activation percentages.

Internuclear ophthalmoplegia — neuroanatomy reference

Clinical correlation: A unilateral MLF lesion impairs adduction of the ipsilateral eye during contralateral horizontal gaze, commonly with abducting nystagmus of the fellow eye. The published figure focuses on pontine circuitry and does not depict every component of the clinical examination.
